title: Songs and Sonnets
description: The collective title given in the 1633 posthumous Poems to Donne's lyrics of love — 'The Good-Morrow', 'The Sun Rising', 'The Canonization', 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning', 'The Ecstasy', 'The Flea', and some fifty more — in which the conventions of Petrarchan love are re-forged by argument, paradox, and the new 'metaphysical' wit.
plot_or_argument: No single plot: the poems dramatize the phases of love — waking, parting, quarrelling, dying, transcending — each lyric a miniature drama of persuasion in which a lover argues a mistress, a rival, the sun, or himself into a truth about love.
narrative_structure: A group of some fifty-five lyrics gathered posthumously under a title Donne never gave them, arranged in the 1633 edition as a loose anthology of the love poems.
principal_characters: the poet-lover; the beloved (unnamed); the Sun; Death; God (in the religious lyrics)
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic, speech-like rhythms within stanza forms of Donne's own devising — the 'strong lines' of the metaphysical manner, with conceits drawn from astronomy, alchemy, law, and cartography.
historical_context: Written from the 1590s (the 'Jack Donne' of Lincoln's Inn and the Essex and Ralegh voyages) into his middle years, circulating in manuscript among the wits and Inns of Court; printed only after his death in the 1633 Poems.
literary_significance: The founding book of metaphysical poetry — the lyric revolution that Jonson's classicism answered and that the twentieth century would re-canonize.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the group's composition dates span at least two decades, and individual datings are widely disputed.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in Poems, by J.D., 1633. Standard edition: John Donne: The Complete English Poems, ed. A. J. Smith (Penguin, 1971); Robin Robbins (ed.), The Complete Poems of John Donne (Longman, 2010).

title: Elegies
description: Donne's love elegies, modelled on Ovid's Amores: some twenty poems in which the speaker moves through the bedrooms, streets, and jealous households of an erotic London — 'The Perfume', 'The Anagram', 'To His Mistress Going to Bed', 'The Change' — with a frankness and irony that scandalized and defined the genre in English.
plot_or_argument: The elegies dramatize an erotic career: seduction, jealousy, constancy debated, the farewell, the anatomy of love's changes — each poem an argumentative scene in the Ovidian manner, from the perfumed lover detected to the mistress commanded 'License my roving hands'.
narrative_structure: A group of poems in the classical elegy form, not a sequence, gathered posthumously; individual poems circulated widely in manuscript from the mid-1590s.
principal_characters: the poet-lover; the mistresses; the rival; the husband; the father (in 'The Perfume')
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets of colloquial force — Ovid's couplet crossed with the speech of the Inns of Court — with enjambment and parenthesis as the instruments of wit.
historical_context: Written in the 1590s, the decade of the English Ovidian vogue and of the 1599 ban that burned Marlowe's and Marston's elegiac verse; Donne's elegies circulated in manuscript and were printed in 1633.
literary_significance: The most powerful English answer to Ovid's Amores and the seedbed of the Restoration's libertine couplet.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the canon and order of the elegies vary among the early manuscripts.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in Poems, 1633. Standard edition: Robin Robbins (ed.), The Complete Poems of John Donne (Longman, 2010).

title: Holy Sonnets
description: Donne's nineteen divine sonnets — 'Batter my heart, three-personed God', 'Death be not proud', 'At the round earth's imagined corners', 'Since she whom I loved hath paid her last debt' — in which the erotic and argumentative energies of the love poems are turned on God, sin, death, and the soul's terror of damnation.
plot_or_argument: The sonnets dramatize the soul's wrestling with God: pleas for violent grace, meditations on death and judgment, griefs of bereavement, and the final sonnets' fear and love of a God who must be wooed with the poet's whole art.
narrative_structure: A cycle of nineteen sonnets (in the standard canon; twelve in the earliest manuscript group, with the later 'Westmoreland' sequence adding the rest), not a plotted sequence but a linked series of meditations.
principal_characters: the speaker; God (as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit); Death; the soul; the angels
meter_and_prosody: The Italian and English sonnet forms strained to the breaking point — spondaic openings, abrupt turns, and the metaphysical conceit turned to devotion.
historical_context: Composed chiefly between 1609 and 1619, the years of Donne's ordination (1615) and of his wife's death (1617); the poems circulated in manuscript and were printed posthumously in 1633.
literary_significance: The supreme English devotional sonnets — the bridge from the Elizabethan love sonnet to the sacred poetry of Herbert, Crashaw, and Hopkins.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the canon of nineteen and the ordering are the work of later editors, from the manuscript groups.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in Poems, 1633. Standard edition: Robin Robbins (ed.), The Complete Poems of John Donne (Longman, 2010).

title: The Anniversaries
alternative_titles: Of the Progress of the Soul
description: Donne's two commemorative poems for Elizabeth Drury, the fifteen-year-old daughter of his patron Sir Robert Drury, who died in 1610: 'An Anatomy of the World' (1611) and 'Of the Progress of the Soul' (1612) — cosmic elegies in which the girl's death becomes the death of the world's coherence, her virtue the measure of its decay, and her translation to heaven the poem's only consolation.
plot_or_argument: The First Anniversary anatomizes the world's sickness — 'new philosophy calls all in doubt' — and finds in the dead girl the pattern of lost virtue; the Second follows her soul's progress beyond the corrupt world to the joys of heaven, ending with the praise of the 'she' whose worth the world could not hold.
narrative_structure: Two linked poems of several hundred couplets each, built as formal 'anatomies' — the dissection of the world, then the itinerary of the soul — with the funerary apparatus of elegies and epitaphs.
principal_characters: Elizabeth Drury (the subject); the poet as anatomist; the World; the Soul; Death
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets of extraordinary intellectual density, with the famous passage on the 'new philosophy' as its centre of gravity.
historical_context: Written 1611–12 in the household of Sir Robert Drury, whose patronage they repaid with a hyperbole that scandalized Ben Jonson; the poems register the crisis of cosmology after Copernicus, Kepler, and Galileo.
literary_significance: The great English poems of the scientific revolution's first shock — and the most extreme test of the elegy's power to make a private grief cosmic.
bibliographical_notes: The First Anniversary, 1611; The Second Anniversary, 1612. Standard edition: Robin Robbins (ed.), The Complete Poems of John Donne (Longman, 2010).

title: Devotions upon Emergent Occasions
description: Donne's prose-and-prayer record of the near-fatal 'spotted fever' he suffered in December 1623, while Dean of St Paul's: twenty-three 'devotions', each in three parts — a Meditation on his sickness and the soul's, an Expostulation with God, and a Prayer — including the seventeenth, whose Meditation contains the most famous passage of his prose: 'No man is an island... for whom the bell tolls'.
plot_or_argument: The book follows the stages of the illness — its first seizure, the physicians' consultations, the crisis, the convalescence — each stage becoming an emblem of the soul's disease and God's physic, from the opening meditation on man's miserable condition to the closing prayer of thankfulness.
narrative_structure: Twenty-three numbered devotions in strict tripartite form (Meditation, Expostulation, Prayer), each anchored to a moment of the illness — the tolling bell of the seventeenth marking the imagined death and burial.
principal_characters: the sick man (Donne); God; the Physicians; the bell
meter_and_prosody: Prose of the pulpit raised to art — the long periodic sentences, antitheses, and paradoxes of Donne's sermons compressed into the private page.
historical_context: Written after the illness of late 1623 and published early in 1624; its great theme — sickness as the soul's education — belongs to Donne's last decade as Dean of St Paul's and the great plague years of Jacobean London.
literary_significance: The classic of English devotional prose, whose 'No man is an island' meditation and 'for whom the bell tolls' have passed into the common language of mortality.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Thomas Jones, 1624. Standard edition: Anthony Raspa (ed.), Devotions upon Emergent Occasions (Oxford, 1987).

title: Satires
description: Donne's five formal verse satires of the 1590s — on the foppish courtier, the corrupt lawyer, religion and the quest for true church, the court, and the suitors and officers of the law — the poems that established the English formal satire and prompted the 1599 ban on satires, with their Juvenalian 'railing' and their portrait of Elizabethan London's vices.
plot_or_argument: Each satire is a walk through a vice — the courtier's affectations, the lawyer's bribes, the sects' errors, the court's vanity, the law's extortion — with the poet as reluctant companion and ironist, and the third satire's 'On a huge hill, / Cragged and steep, Truth stands' as the sequence's moral summit.
narrative_structure: Five numbered satires in the formal Roman manner, each a single scene or progress through the city, in the couplet form Donne hardened into an instrument of speech.
principal_characters: the satirist; the fop; the lawyer; the courtier; the officers and suitors
meter_and_prosody: Rough, deliberately harsh heroic couplets — 'strong lines' — whose jagged enjambment and parenthesis imitated the speech of the town and the Roman satirists' abruptness.
historical_context: Written 1593–98, in the decade that also produced the satires of Hall and Marston; the bishops' ban of 1599, which ordered the burning of satires, answered this vogue directly.
literary_significance: The foundation of English formal satire — the model for Pope's couplet and for every later poet of the town's vices.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in Poems, 1633. Standard edition: Robin Robbins (ed.), The Complete Poems of John Donne (Longman, 2010).

title: A Book of Airs
description: The songbook of 1601 by Thomas Campion (words and music) and Philip Rosseter (music): twenty-one lute songs and one masque song, including 'My sweetest Lesbia', 'Follow thy fair sun', 'When to her lute Corinna sings', and 'I care not for these ladies' — the volume that made Campion the supreme English lyricist of the lute-song golden age.
plot_or_argument: No plot: the airs set the commonplaces of love — carpe diem, the lady's beauty, the lover's complaint, the joys of country over court — each song a perfected miniature in the courtly lyric tradition.
narrative_structure: A printed songbook of twenty-one airs plus the masque song, arranged for voice and lute (some also for viol consort), in the standard format of the English ayre books.
principal_characters: the singer-lover; Lesbia; Corinna; the beloved ladies
meter_and_prosody: Short-line lyric stanzas of exquisite finish — trochees, iambs, and the quantitative experiments of Campion's 'observations' — composed for music and printed with tablature.
historical_context: Published 1601 in the first great decade of the English ayre, alongside Dowland's and Jones's books; Campion's preface defends the new union of English verse and music against the metrical pedants.
literary_significance: The classic of the Elizabethan lute-song tradition — poetry and music fused as nowhere else in the language, and a touchstone for every later English lyricist.
attribution_notes: Words by Campion throughout, with one masque song; music by Campion for half the airs and by Rosseter for the rest.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Peter Short, 1601. Standard edition: The Works of Thomas Campion, ed. Walter R. Davis (New York, 1967).

title: Nosce Teipsum
description: Sir John Davies's philosophical poem on the immortality of the soul: 'Know thyself' — the soul's nature, its faculties, its independence from the body, and the proofs of its immortality — argued in some 2,000 lines of didactic couplets, the poem that made Davies famous overnight and earned him the favour of James I.
plot_or_argument: The poem proceeds from the Delphic command through the soul's definition, its powers of sense, fancy, and reason, the distinction of soul and body, the refutation of the soul's mortality, and the closing proof of its divine origin and destiny — a scholastic summa rendered in verse.
narrative_structure: Two books of sustained didactic argument, each section a step in the proof, with the famous passage on the soul's 'infinity of desire' as its centre.
principal_characters: the poet as philosopher; the Soul; Reason; the Body
meter_and_prosody: Iambic pentameter couplets of a clear, dry, argumentative elegance — the manner that would become the Augustan couplet's parent.
historical_context: Published 1599, in the same years as Donne's satires and the philosophical poems of the Inns of Court; Davies, a lawyer who became Attorney General for Ireland, dedicated it to Elizabeth I, and its success made his reputation at both courts.
literary_significance: The most accomplished English philosophical poem of its generation and a direct ancestor of the Augustan poetry of statement.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Richard Field, 1599. Standard edition: The Poems of Sir John Davies, ed. Robert Krueger (Oxford, 1975).
